body_html:
Note:

Since my trade alert on Monday, the shares are down to $59, so the upside is now 74% with a risk-reward of 1 to 3.2. Even better!

My top three positions that have 5x to 8x1 are AI-related holdings, POWL and STRL, crossed +1,000% last week.

That kind of move is the privilege of buying right and sitting still, but it also concentrates the portfolio in one theme. Almost a fifth of the portfolio (6 companies out of a total of 31) are related to the AI-theme. All those positions have appreciated considerably. The one with the smallest gain is MU, which has gained 106% from the cost basis…

… or 136% since I recommended it the first time.

So while 19% of the positions are in the AI-theme on a count basis, 38.3% of the market value of the portfolio is in the theme.

So I’ve been hunting in sectors I actually understand, away from the AI complex. Energy first. In November, I flagged in the Weekly 58 that energy was the sector to watch on a 12-month view.

In December, I followed with my first energy pick…

… and in March, I added a second energy name in MENA oilfield services.

Utilities second. In February I picked up a utility name that slipped through my fingers in 2024 when valuation finally became sensible.

Defence third. My April defence pick sits on the +13.4% FY2026 budget signal and a multi-year spend cycle.

So far, 3 out of my 4 picks show a positive return. Defence shows a loss, but it hasn’t been more than a month yet.

So which space will be the fourth???

Food is the fourth, and the logic looks like defence: regulatory tailwinds doing the work, multiples compressed, and the operating story turning before the multiple does. Of every food name I’ve looked at over the past month, this one is the one I keep coming back to.

Why Food, Why Now

I’ve spent the past quarter looking at every credible food name with a circular-economy or biofuel angle. Adecoagro. Bunge. ADM. Bachoco. Pilgrim’s Pride (which I just exited).

Of all of them, this one has the most asymmetric setup right now because three things are converging at the same time.

  1. A federal regulator finalized the largest renewable fuel mandate in the program’s history.

  2. A pending European joint venture gives the high-margin specialty arm a 12-16x EBITDA re-rating catalyst inside the next 12 months.

  3. And the operations team has spent two years cleaning up two big acquisitions, with the result showing up cleanly in Q1 2026’s gross margin print.

Each of those would be useful on its own. Together, they’re a regime change.

The market hasn’t repriced for this. The stock trades at 14.5x EV/EBITDA versus a 5-year average of 13.5x, slightly above on the surface, but the trough year compresses EBITDA artificially.

On the DCF-implied EV/EBITDA of 20.6x, the entry today is 40% below fair value. P/B at 2.2x versus the 5-year average of 2.1x looks slightly expensive only because book value is depressed.

This company is the unglamorous opposite of an AI compute story. The company picks up dead animals, used fryer oil, and slaughterhouse byproducts from hundreds of thousands of collection points and turns them into proteins, fats, collagen, gelatin, and renewable diesel feedstock. Every part of the supply chain is regulated. Every cent of the margin depends on commodity pricing. The stock has been cut in half from its 2022 highs and is one of the most hated names in consumer staples. It’s exactly the kind of business I want to own when the AI frenzy needs a counterweight.

Table of Contents:

  • TLDR

  • How Does The Company Rank?

  • How Does It Actually Make Money

  • The Pricing Dynamics That Run This Business

  • The Long-Form Thesis

  • Valuation

  • Steel-Manning The Bear

  • Variant Perception

  • Verdict

TLDR

  • Darling Ingredients [DAR] is the world’s largest renderer and the 50% owner of Diamond Green Diesel, the lowest-cost renewable diesel producer in North America.

  • The bull case is a regime change in renewable fuel policy: the EPA finalized record 2026-2027 RVOs in March, biomass-based diesel mandates jumped to 8.86B-8.95B gallons, and Q1 2026 was the first quarter where you can see the new pricing regime in DAR’s print (Feed gross margin +500bps y/y, DGD EBITDA per gallon back to $1.11).

  • The Tessenderlo JV, expected to close within 12 months, consolidates PB Leiner’s collagen capacity at 85% DAR ownership and shifts the Food segment toward higher-multiple specialty ingredients. The DGD stake on its own is worth $2.9B in my central case (vs $2.1B carrying value), with a probability-weighted range of $1.0B (bear) to $4.8B (bull). That alone is $5/share of unrecognized asset value.

  • The key risk is commodity price reversal. My Monte Carlo (3,500 simulations across volume, price, gross margin, WACC, and DGD JV stake value) shows 19% of observations leave the equity at zero, and 64% are below today’s share price. Price growth is 60% of the variance, and gross margin is another 18%.

  • My DCF target is $103 (+65% from the current $62). Risk-reward is 1 to 2.9 against the $48 bear case. Buy.

Below is the long-form thesis. Why food now, why this name, where the bear case is strongest, and what the model says.

How Does The Company Rank?

Before the deep dive, here’s how DAR scores on RankedStocks.com. The composite RS score is 85 (top quartile), with Country and Sector percentiles both at 89%. DAR ranks in the top 11% of US-listed Consumer Staples names by the platform’s framework. The factor breakdown:

Valuation: 11. The platform reads DAR as expensive on factor scoring. This is consistent with EV/EBITDA at 14.5x sitting slightly above the 5-year average of 13.5x. The framework penalizes the surface multiple even though the trough EBITDA distorts the read.

Growth: 86. Strong revenue and earnings growth profile, anchored to the 5-year revenue CAGR of 2.9% (acquisition-heavy) plus the 2026-2027 RVO and Tessenderlo JV step-ups locked into the forecast.

Profitability: 78. Solid margin and capital-efficiency profile despite the 2025 trough. Q1 2026 gross margin of 26.1% is +350bps y/y.

Sentiment: 93. Excellent. Analyst revisions and market positioning have turned constructive post-RVO finalization.

Outlook: 88. Forward-looking expectations are well-supported. Multi-year visibility from the 2026-2027 RVO, the Tessenderlo close, and the Patense bolt-on.

The takeaway: top-quartile composite score driven by Sentiment, Outlook, and Growth, held back only by the Valuation factor that reads the surface multiple without distinguishing between trough EBITDA and normalized earnings power. That gap between the platform read and the DCF-implied multiple is exactly the asymmetry I’m buying.

How Does It Actually Make Money

Darling runs three reporting segments and a 50% JV. The segments share the same raw material (animal byproducts, used cooking oil, bakery waste) but route the molecules into different markets. The JV, Diamond Green Diesel, is a separate entity 50% owned with Valero. Most analysts focus on DGD because the gallons-per-quarter numbers are big and the policy headlines are loud. That’s a mistake. The core ingredients business is where the moat lives.

Feed Ingredients (~65% of revenue)

This is the rendering business. DAR collects raw material from slaughterhouses, butchers, restaurants, and supermarkets. The scale is enormous: 12.7M metric tons processed in FY2025, across more than 250 plants in over 15 countries. The output is fats (tallow, yellow grease, poultry fat), proteins (meat-and-bone meal, poultry meal, feather meal), used cooking oil, and bakery byproducts.

The fats either sell into the renewable diesel feedstock market (mostly to DGD itself) or into oleochemicals. The proteins go into pet food, aquaculture, and livestock feed. UCO has become its own category as biofuel demand has pushed grease prices up. In Q1 2026 the Feed segment booked $985M in net sales on flat 3.1M tons of raw material processed, meaning the entire +9.9% y/y revenue growth was price. Gross margin expanded from 20.3% in Q1 2025 to 25.3% in Q1 2026, a +500bps move that the market has not yet credited.

Look at the blue line in the chart below. It shows sustained gross margin improvement for the feed segment as fat prices moved higher and operations stabilized.

The economics here are simple: DAR pays renderers a contracted price for raw material (formula-linked, with 30-60 day lags), runs it through high-temperature cookers to separate fats from proteins, and sells the finished products at spot or contract pricing. Spread management is the entire game. When fat prices rise faster than raw material payments, gross margin expands. When fat prices fall, it compresses. The lags work in DAR’s favour on the way up and against it on the way down.

Food Ingredients (~25% of revenue)

This is the collagen and gelatin business, primarily run through the Rousselot brand and the Gelnex acquisition (Brazil-based, picked up in 2023). DAR is now the world’s largest collagen producer. The product range goes from commodity gelatin (sweets, capsules, photographic film) to hydrolyzed collagen (nutraceuticals, sports supplements, “food as medicine” applications) to specialty branded products like Peptan and Nextida.

The Tessenderlo JV, signed in December 2025 and currently in antitrust review, will consolidate PB Leiner (Tessenderlo’s gelatin and collagen subsidiary) into a NewCo with Darling owning 85%. PB Leiner adds significant European and Latin American capacity. The CFO was explicit on the Q1 2026 call: the JV is the lever that takes Food segment EBITDA into the 12-16x multiple range that specialty health and nutrition businesses get.

Q1 2026 Food sales were $405M (+16% y/y) on flat volume. Gross margin printed at 28.9%, down marginally from 29.3% a year ago but well above the 25-27% range it ran at in 2022-2023. The Nextida product line, which positions hydrolyzed collagen as a non-pharmaceutical glucose-control alternative to GLP-1 drugs, is starting to drive repeat orders.

Fuel Ingredients (~10% of revenue, and the entire DGD story)

Two distinct businesses are bundled into this segment. Reported segment net sales are bioenergy only: Ecoson and Rendac in Europe, where DAR runs anaerobic digesters that turn organic waste into biogas, plus a few smaller US operations. That business booked $160M in Q1 2026 sales on 370k tons of raw material, with gross margin of 24.1%. It’s a stable annuity-like contributor with European energy price tailwinds.

DGD is the headline. It’s a 1.3 billion gallon nameplate renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel facility, 50% owned by Darling and 50% by Valero, located at Valero’s St. Charles and Port Arthur refineries on the US Gulf Coast. DGD is the lowest-cost RD producer in North America because it sources cheap low-CI feedstock (UCO, animal fat, distiller’s corn oil) from DAR’s own rendering network, bypasses pretreatment for those feedstocks, and shares utilities with the Valero refineries.

DGD’s earnings flow through to DAR as equity income, not consolidated revenue. In Q1 2026 DGD generated $1.11 of EBITDA per gallon on 272M gallons sold, contributing $151M to Darling’s bottom line. That EBITDA per gallon was zero in Q4 2024 and just $0.21 for full-year 2025. Q1 2026 is the first clean print of the new RVO regime.

The Pricing Dynamics That Run This Business

If you only have time to understand one thing about Darling, understand the spread between feedstock prices and renewable fuel margins. That spread is the entire investable story. It’s set by three things working together: federal renewable fuel policy, state low-carbon fuel programs, and the global price of soybean oil and palm oil that act as substitutes.

The 2026-2027 RVO is the largest mandate in the program’s history

The EPA finalized the 2026 and 2027 Renewable Fuel Standard volumes on March 27, 2026. Total renewable fuel was set at 26.81B gallons in 2026 and 27.02B in 2027, both record highs. Biomass-based diesel, the category that includes DGD’s renewable diesel, was set at 8.86B gallons in 2026 and 8.95B in 2027, rising to 9.07B and 9.20B once small refinery exemption reallocations are layered in.

That step-up matters because the prior 2024-2025 RVO never ramped fast enough to absorb the renewable diesel capacity that was built ahead of it. The result was a 2024-2025 supply glut, RIN prices that collapsed, and DGD running at sub-economic margins. The 2026-2027 RVO inverts that. The CFO said on the Q1 2026 call: “RINs need to play their role in all that to be the great equalizer that creates a good renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel margin.” Translation: with the higher mandate, RINs have to clear higher to incentivize the production needed to fill the obligation.

Feedstock prices are tracking exactly what you’d expect

Yellow grease and bleachable fancy tallow, the two prices that matter most for DAR’s Feed segment, were $36.63/cwt and $59.53/cwt average in Q1 2026, with March alone printing $40.30 and $66.07. April pricing reportedly accelerated further. The CEO mentioned on the Q1 2026 call that “the DGD bid right now today is close to $0.80 a pound” for fat, up $0.20 to $0.25 from Q4 2025 levels.

Soybean oil, the substitute that drags fat prices with it, hit $0.59/lb in the April 2026 WASDE forecast, the highest since summer 2023. The USDA explicitly cited “high petroleum prices and final EPA Renewable Volume Obligation standards” as the drivers. California’s biomass-based diesel share of the state’s diesel pool went from 25% in 2020 to over 70% in the first three quarters of 2025, which gives you a sense of how dependent the West Coast fuel system has become on this category.

Why imports can’t fix the supply gap

The bear case for years has been “fine, but cheap imports of UCO and tallow will fill the new mandate, capping fat prices.” Two things broke that argument. First, Trump imposed origin tariffs on imported feedstocks, particularly Chinese UCO and Brazilian tallow. Second, the proposed half-RIN treatment for foreign feedstocks (effective 2028) creates a structural premium for domestic supply.

I think with a 50% RIN on foreign feedstocks, US domestic feedstocks become the only scalable way to fill a 9 billion gallon biomass-based diesel mandate.

The math doesn’t work otherwise. US tallow and yellow grease total annual production is roughly 4 billion pounds. UCO collection is around 1.5 billion pounds. Combined that’s about 700M gallons of renewable diesel equivalent. The rest of the mandate has to come from soybean oil (the marginal feedstock), distiller’s corn oil, and imports. The price-clearing mechanism has to push fat prices high enough to disincentivize other uses (animal feed, oleochemicals) and pull every available pound into fuel.

Collagen demand is on its own secular curve

Food doesn’t depend on the RVO at all. Hydrolyzed collagen is forecast to grow at a 11.9% CAGR through 2030, with the broader collagen market growing 5.8-9.3% depending on the source.

The drivers are nutraceuticals (45% of demand and growing), food and beverage applications, and the GLP-1-adjacent supplement category that Darling’s Nextida product targets. Gelatin demand is more cyclical but has stabilized after the 2022-2024 destocking that hit the segment hard. Q1 2026 commentary from the CEO was that “demand has been worked through pretty much around the world” and that gelatin margins are now improving.

If the JV closes on the expected timeline, Darling becomes the world’s largest hydrolyzed collagen producer at 85% ownership, with capacity that doesn’t need a renewable diesel mandate to work.

The Long-Form Thesis

Leg #1. DGD is the lowest-cost producer at the exact moment the mandate forces marginal capacity to clear higher

DGD’s structural cost advantage runs on three things.

  1. First, it sources roughly 60% of its feedstock from DAR’s own rendering network, which means it gets cheap low-CI material at internal transfer pricing rather than at spot.

  2. Second, it doesn’t need pretreatment for animal fat and UCO (a capability competitors using soybean oil require), which saves capex and opex.

  3. Third, the plants are co-located with Valero refineries, so it shares hydrogen, utilities, and logistics infrastructure.

The Q1 2026 print was the first clean look at what that looks like in the new regime. EBITDA per gallon hit $1.11. DGD is running close to maximum capacity Q2 2026 guidance is 320M gallons, “pretty close to full out” as the CFO said during the call.

My industry channel checks suggest competitor renewable diesel facilities running on soybean oil are operating below cash break-even at current RIN prices, which is why so much US capacity is still idle. With the RVO regime forcing margins higher to bring that capacity back, DGD captures a disproportionate share of the new economics because it’s first in the merit order. Every dollar of margin expansion in the industry flows disproportionately to the lowest-cost operator.

Leg #2. The regulatory regime moved from ambiguous to anchored, and the market hasn’t repriced

The 2026-2027 RVO is the largest in the program’s history. The production tax credit under 45Z monetizes domestic feedstocks at a premium that gets even larger when the proposed half-RIN treatment for foreign feedstocks kicks in from 2028. DAR sold $285M of PTC in 2025 at strong realization rates because DGD converted to R-100 production faster than peers, qualifying it for direct PTC monetization while competitors had to sell at a discount.

The durability question matters. This regime is more durable than the pre-2026 RFS because the volumes were set explicitly at levels that require imports plus domestic capacity working hard; the half-RIN proposal forces more value to the North American supply, and bipartisan support around energy security has held even through the 2024 election cycle.

The bear case is that a future administration could unwind the RVO, but the path to do so is procedurally hard and the political cost is high (rural-state jobs, diesel prices, energy security). The two-year visibility is locked in. The 2028+ regime is a real risk worth pricing, but not a 2026 risk.

Leg #3. The Tessenderlo JV is a forced re-rating event for the Food segment

The PB Leiner consolidation moves the Food segment EBITDA into a 12-16x multiple bracket that the rest of Darling’s businesses don’t get. The CFO has been explicit that if the market doesn’t recognize that multiple internally, the company will look at structural options to surface the value. Translation: spin, sale, or separate listing. Definitive agreements were signed in December 2025. Antitrust review is in process and management expects to close within 12 months.

PB Leiner’s revenue contribution is in the $400-500M range and the Darling consolidation is at 85%, which adds roughly $350M to Food segment revenue at full run rate.

The deal will close because antitrust on collagen has historically been clean and the PB Leiner business is a willing seller. Once it’s in the run rate, the segment is too big to be valued at the same blended rendering multiple as the rest of Darling. The market is pricing zero of this re-rating today. When the close hits, that changes mechanically.

Underneath all three: operational excellence finally landing, balance sheet on a clear deleveraging path

The 2022-2023 acquisitions (Valley Proteins for $1.1B, FASA for $635M, Gelnex for $150M) loaded DAR with integration work that depressed margins for two years. The work is done. Q1 2026 is the first quarter where you can see the post-integration margin profile cleanly: Feed gross margin sequential progression of 20.3% → 22.9% → 24.3% → 24.6% → 25.3%.

The CFO attributed the improvement to “operations and sort of understanding how these assets all fit together... manifesting themselves most right now in the form of the high-quality proteins that we’re making and the premiums we’re able to capture.” Capex/D&A ratio in 2025 was 0.78x, indicating the asset base is now being maintained rather than expanded, which frees up FCF.

The balance sheet was the constraint for two years. Net debt of $4.0B at Q1 2026 with a leverage ratio of 3.17x bank covenant is uncomfortable but inside the 4.5x covenant threshold. The CFO has stated explicitly that the priority is paying down debt to under $3B before considering buybacks, M&A, or dividends. The next Weekly will talk about net leverage and cyclical companies, very relevant for DAR.

With the RVO regime supporting EBITDA expansion and DGD distributions, the deleveraging path is clear. By the end of FY2026 the company should be inside its target range, opening up capital allocation optionality that doesn’t exist today.

Valuation

The DCF model is the centre of the valuation work. I’ve spent the last two weeks walking through every input on the model with my own assumptions, and the output is a fair share price of $103. That’s +65% upside on the central case, with risk-reward of 1 to 2.9 against a $48 bear case.

View DCF here

What the model assumes

The revenue build is segment-by-segment, with volume and price split out separately.

Feed grows total revenue at +10% in 2026 (Patense bolt-on plus the post-RVO price tailwind) before tapering to +2.5% steady state by 2030. Food grows +12% in 2026 and +11% in 2027 as the Tessenderlo JV consolidates, then +4% organic thereafter as the Nextida specialty mix continues to ramp. Fuel (the bioenergy line) grows +8% in 2026 on European energy prices, then +3.5% steady state. The aggregate revenue trajectory takes total sales from $6.14B in FY2025 to $10.28B in FY2037, a 4.4% CAGR.

Gross margin assumptions reflect the structural improvement story. Feed at 24.0% in 2026 (anchored to the Q1 25.3% print, moderated for full-year mix) and 23.5% steady state. Food at 28.0% in 2026, dipping to 27.0% in 2027-2028 as PB Leiner’s commodity gelatin mix dilutes the blend, then drifting back to 28.0% by 2034 as Nextida ramps. Fuel at 21.0% in 2026 and 20.0% LT. The blended consolidated gross margin lands at 24.7% in 2026 versus the 24.0% FY2025 actual.

SG&A intensity glides from 9.0% of revenue in 2025 to 8.0% by 2037, capturing operating leverage on a stable corporate footprint.

Capex intensity is held at 6.0% near term and steps up to 6.5% in the back half because compliance capex is structurally rising (from 12% of total in 2023 to 24% in 2025) and rendering equipment maintenance is heavy.

Working capital is held at 51-day cash cycle (39 days receivables + 41 days inventory minus 29 days payables), which matches the 2025 run rate after the Valley Proteins/FASA destocking finished. The tax rate is 25% in 2026 (the CFO’s explicit guide on the Q1 26 call) and 24% steady state, reflecting the federal-plus-state-plus-foreign blend less a modest PTC tailwind.

WACC is 6.40%, built from a cost of equity of 8.80% (4.38% risk-free, 4.23% MRP, 1.05 levered beta) and a cost of debt of 4.5% at a 45% optimal debt-to-capital. Terminal growth in NOPAT is 3.0%, broadly in line with global GDP plus a modest premium for the company’s circular-economy mix.

The DGD JV stake valued separately, then added back

The model treats the core ingredients business and the DGD JV separately, using proper sum-of-the-parts logic. The consolidated DCF runs the discounted cash flows on the core business only (Feed, Food, and bioenergy), with the DGD equity income line stripped out. The DGD JV stake is then added back as a discrete investment line at $2,958M, which is the Base Case from a capitalized through-cycle EBITDA framework. Three lenses triangulate to that valuation: capitalized EBITDA, per-gallon transaction comp, and replacement cost. The $2.96B base-case stake compares to a $2.1B carrying value on the balance sheet, so the model is already giving credit for roughly $5/share of DGD asset value above book.

Using the capitalized EBITDA approach with three regime scenarios: bear (sustained 2024-25 trough at $0.25/gal × 1.3B gallons × 6.5x multiple) gives Darling’s 50% stake at $1.0B. Base (mid-cycle post-RVO at $0.65/gal × 1.3B × 7.0x) gives $2.9B. Bull (Q1 26 print holds at $1.00/gal × 1.3B × 7.5x) gives $4.8B. Probability-weight 30% bear / 50% base / 20% bull, and the central stake value is roughly $2.8B, or +$5/share above book.

The bull case (Q1 2026 margins hold at $1.00/gal) would lift the JV stake to $4.8B and add roughly +$12/share to fair value above the $103 target. The bear case (sustained 2024-25 trough at $0.25/gal) drops it to $1.0B and would cut the target by about $12/share. The base case is already in the $103 number.

Where I might be wrong

Two assumptions carry most of the model’s NPV. The first is the price growth schedule in Feed (+7% in 2026, +2% in 2027, +1.5% LT). The second is the terminal margin profile (Feed 23.5%, Food 28%, Fuel 20%). Move either by 100bps and the target shifts $8 to $12. Move WACC by 50bps and the target shifts $7. The model is more sensitive to operating assumptions than to the discount rate.

Monte Carlo

On a side note, my Monte Carlo Simulator add-on just got approved! You can download it by clicking here.

I ran 3,500 Monte Carlo simulations across five inputs to stress-test the central case. The input distributions:

  • Volume growth: mean 1.5%, std dev 1.5% (organic-only steady state).

  • Price growth: mean 1.0%, std dev 4.0% (high uncertainty around the dominant driver).

  • Gross margin: mean 22.0%, std dev 3.0% (cycle-aware terminal anchor).

  • WACC: mean 7.0%, std dev 1.0% (slightly above current 6.4% to test discount-rate sensitivity).

  • DGD JV stake: discrete distribution: bear $1.0B (30%), base $2.9B (50%), bull $4.8B (20%).

Three numbers from the simulation matter.

First, 19% of observations leave the equity at or below zero. It’s a statement that under a wide enough range of price-growth and margin assumptions, the DCF math produces zero or negative equity value. The base business is leveraged enough (3.17x at Q1 26) that a sustained period of weak fat prices and compressed renewable diesel margins eats the equity.

Second, 64% of observations come out below today’s price. The current market price sits in the right tail of the simulation distribution, not the centre.

Third, the variance decomposition tells you which assumptions matter most: price growth is 60% of the variance, gross margin is 18%, WACC is 11%, volume growth 9%, and the DGD JV stake just 2%.

The simulation is telling you the same thing the bear case has been telling you for three years: this is a price taker, not a price maker, and the entire equity story rides on whether the policy and commodity regime supports prices. What’s different now versus 2023-2025 is that the regime variable is no longer ambiguous. The RVO is finalized, the PTC is monetizable, the half-RIN proposal is in the pipeline, and the Q1 2026 print is the first clean data point of the new regime. The 60% price-sensitivity that hurt for two years now cuts the other way.

Steel-Manning The Bear

The bear case on DAR is not a list of generic concerns. It’s a coherent argument that this is structurally a low-multiple commodity processor whose entire equity value is hostage to two policy variables and one commodity price. Walk through the strongest version of it.

First, the RVO can be unwound. The 2026-2027 mandate was set by an EPA administrator working under a Republican administration that has been explicitly supportive of biofuels for energy security reasons. Administrations change. The 2032 mandate, when it comes up, could be set materially lower. There is also the small refinery exemption mechanism, which can be expanded to effectively reduce mandate enforcement without a public rule change. The RVO that looks anchored today might be a four-year window, not a structural regime.

Second, feedstock substitution is a real cap on fat prices. Soybean oil at $0.59/lb is competing with tallow at roughly $0.72/lb (Q1 2026 average). If fat prices push much higher, the marginal renewable diesel producer switches more aggressively to soy and corn oil, and the fat premium compresses. The CEO acknowledged this on the Q1 2026 call: “DGD is well setup to maximize opportunities depending on what is the lowest cost, net of CI score, feedstock and run for that barrel. That implies that there’s an increase in the utilization of veg oils into the mix.” If even DGD is running more soy, the floor on fat prices is lower than the bull case suggests.

Third, DGD’s economics depend on a partner whose strategic priorities can shift. Valero owns the other 50% and operates the plants. Valero’s first priority is its own refining business, not maximizing DGD’s earnings. If Valero ever decides DGD is a non-core asset (a real possibility given the volatility of renewable fuel margins), the JV could be unwound at a price that doesn’t capture the optionality I’m assuming. There’s no contractual mechanism that forces Valero to keep DGD running at maximum throughput if conventional diesel margins look better on a given day.

Fourth, the Tessenderlo JV could run into antitrust trouble in Europe, particularly because PB Leiner and Rousselot together would have a dominant share of the European gelatin market. The deal could be modified, delayed past the 12-month window, or required to divest assets that erode the strategic logic. The 12-16x multiple uplift the CFO is targeting depends on the deal closing as structured.

Fifth, leverage matters at the wrong moment. At 3.17x bank covenant, DAR has room above the 4.5x covenant threshold, but a 12-month period of compressed margins could chew through that buffer faster than the deleveraging plan recovers it. The Q1 2026 working-capital contribution to DGD pulled the ratio up sharply; another quarter or two of similar dynamics would force conservative capital allocation choices.

Beyond those five risks, there’s the JBS-style governance overhang. Darling has had control-premium speculation in the past, and the controlling family-aligned shareholders could pursue a transaction that surfaces value at a price below the DCF. Buyout protection is not a thesis driver, but if any of the five risks above starts to bite, a forced sale at a depressed multiple is the path of least resistance.

Variant Perception

The market is treating DAR as a leveraged renewable diesel proxy. That framing made sense in 2024-2025 when the entire stock was a directional bet on RIN prices. It’s wrong now. Three things have changed that the market hasn’t repriced.

The first is that Food and Feed are converging on a structurally higher gross margin profile than they ran at in 2022-2024, independent of RVO. The Q1 2026 print confirmed this. The second is that the Tessenderlo JV is going to surface the Food segment as a separate valuation lens, which changes how a sum-of-the-parts approach lands. The third is that the RVO is now anchored, the PTC is monetized, and the half-RIN proposal protects domestic feedstock value structurally. The thing the market has been waiting for has happened, but the multiple still trades at the level it ran at when the regime was uncertain.

The variant view is that Darling at $63 is being priced as a 2024 stock, not a 2026 stock. The catalyst for repricing is the second-quarter 2026 print and the Tessenderlo JV close, both of which are inside the next 9 months.

Verdict

I’m a buyer with a target of $103. Risk-reward is 1 to 2.9 on the central case and considerably wider on the right tail. This isn’t a bet on Darling executing perfectly. It’s a bet on a policy regime that has already changed pricing through a market that hasn’t repriced yet.

1

Last week it was more like 11x, but the market is down this week, as you know, for those names.
